questions.question: Explain how the migrant labour system on the gold mines worked and why the mining companies preferred it.
questions.expected_answer: By 1910 about 200 000 black workers, almost all migrants, worked on contracts of months to a year or more, lived in single-sex compounds and returned home, many repeatedly. They came from the Eastern Cape, Natal and Zululand, Lesotho, Botswana, Eswatini, the northern Transvaal and especially southern Mozambique, recruited by Wenela. Land loss after conquest, cash taxes, crowded reserves and the 1913 Land Act, limiting African land ownership to about 7 percent, kept people in the system. The companies preferred it because they did not pay for family housing, schools or pensions, could pay a single man's wage because the rural household grew food and supported dependants, and sent sick, injured and old workers home. Pass laws prevented family settlement in towns. Historians say the rural areas subsidised the mines.

questions.question: Describe the effects of migrant labour on women and children in rural areas.
questions.expected_answer: Women took on extra work, such as ploughing, herding, building and dealing with officials, in addition to farming, raising children alone, caring for the sick and old, and fetching water and firewood. They managed remittances and earned cash by brewing, selling vegetables or other work, showing resilience. Children grew up with absent fathers; boys herded cattle young and often became migrants as teenagers; girls did household work early; grandmothers raised many children. Long separations strained marriages, letters were slow and written by others, some men formed new relationships in town and stopped sending money, and some women left their villages. As reserves declined, households depended more on remittances and could fall into poverty when they failed.

questions.question: Explain the effects of migrant labour on health, household income and family structure in the long term.
questions.expected_answer: Health: tuberculosis spread in crowded compounds, worsened by silicosis, and sick workers sent home infected families, so doctors saw TB spreading in the Eastern Cape, Lesotho and Mozambique; injury and death removed the main cash income, and compensation for black workers was small. Income: remittances paid taxes, food in droughts, lobola, ploughs, cattle, school fees and better houses; from 1928 Mozambican workers received part of their pay on return. Structure: many households came to be headed by women, men lived for years in hostels, and apartheid extended the system with pass laws and influx control that kept families apart. The system affected Lesotho, Mozambique, Eswatini, Botswana and Malawi as well as South Africa, and migration between rural areas and cities continues today.
